text: Let [latex]C[/latex] be a clockwise oriented closed curve in the complex plane defined by [latex]|z|=1[/latex]. Further, let [latex]f(z)=j z[/latex] be a complex function, where [latex]j=\sqrt{-1}[/latex]. Then, [latex]\oint_{{C}} {f}({z}) {dz}=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
html:
Let [latex]C[/latex] be a clockwise oriented closed curve in the complex plane defined by [latex]|z|=1[/latex]. Further, let [latex]f(z)=j z[/latex] be a complex function, where [latex]j=\sqrt{-1}[/latex].
Then, [latex]\oint_{{C}} {f}({z}) {dz}=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
explanation_text: Step 1: Express the function We are given [latex] f(z) = jz [/latex], and we want to compute: [latex] \oint_C jz , dz [/latex] Step 2: Use properties of contour integrals [latex] j = \sqrt{-1} [/latex] is a constant, so it can be pulled out of the integral: [latex] \oint_C jz , dz = j \oint_C z , dz [/latex] Step 3: Recall the standard result For a closed contour [latex] C [/latex] enclosing the origin (like [latex] |z| = 1 [/latex]), [latex] \oint_C z , dz = 0 [/latex] because [latex] z [/latex] is an analytic function inside and on [latex] C [/latex]. Step 4: Apply the result [latex] \oint_C f(z) , dz = j \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]
explanation_html:
Step 1: Express the function
We are given [latex] f(z) = jz [/latex], and we want to compute:
[latex] \oint_C jz , dz [/latex]

Step 2: Use properties of contour integrals
[latex] j = \sqrt{-1} [/latex] is a constant, so it can be pulled out of the integral:
[latex] \oint_C jz , dz = j \oint_C z , dz [/latex]

Step 3: Recall the standard result
For a closed contour [latex] C [/latex] enclosing the origin (like [latex] |z| = 1 [/latex]),
[latex] \oint_C z , dz = 0 [/latex] because [latex] z [/latex] is an analytic function inside and on [latex] C [/latex].

Step 4: Apply the result
[latex] \oint_C f(z) , dz = j \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]

text: Consider ordinary differential equations given by [latex]\dot{x}_{1}({t})=2 {x}_{2}({t}) [/latex] [latex] \dot{{x}}_{2}({t})={r}({t})[/latex] with initial conditions [latex]{x}_{1}(0)=1[/latex] and [latex]{x}_{2}(0)=0[/latex]. explanation_text:
Given [latex]\frac{{dx}_{1}}{{dt}}=2 {x}_{2} \quad ...(1)[/latex] [latex]\frac{{dx}_{2}}{{dt}}={r}({t}), \quad {r}({t})=\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: {t} \geq 0 \\ 0: {t} < 0 \end{array}\right.[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \frac{{dx}_{2}}{{dt}}=1[/latex] for [latex]{t} \geq 0 \quad ...(2)[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow {x}_{2}={t}+{c}  \quad ...(3)[/latex] Given [latex]x_{2}(0)=0[/latex] (3) [latex]\Rightarrow 0=0+c \Rightarrow c=0[/latex] [latex]\therefore {x}_{2}={t}[/latex] From (1) [latex]\frac{d x_{1}}{d t}=2 t[/latex] [latex]
\Rightarrow {x}_{1}=\frac{2 {t}^{2}}{2}+{K} \quad ...(4)
[/latex] Given [latex]{x}_{1}(0)=1:(4) \Rightarrow 1=0+{K}[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow {K}=1[/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] From (4) [latex]{x}_{1}={t}^{2}+1[/latex] Now [latex]{X}_{1}(1)=1+1=2[/latex]
explanation_html:
Given [latex]\frac{{dx}_{1}}{{dt}}=2 {x}_{2} \quad ...(1)[/latex]
[latex]\frac{{dx}_{2}}{{dt}}={r}({t}), \quad {r}({t})=\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: {t} \geq 0 \\ 0: {t} < 0 \end{array}\right.[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{{dx}_{2}}{{dt}}=1[/latex] for [latex]{t} \geq 0 \quad ...(2)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow {x}_{2}={t}+{c} \quad ...(3)[/latex]
Given [latex]x_{2}(0)=0[/latex]
(3) [latex]\Rightarrow 0=0+c \Rightarrow c=0[/latex]
[latex]\therefore {x}_{2}={t}[/latex]
From (1) [latex]\frac{d x_{1}}{d t}=2 t[/latex]

[latex]\Rightarrow {K}=1[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] From (4) [latex]{x}_{1}={t}^{2}+1[/latex]
Now [latex]{X}_{1}(1)=1+1=2[/latex]

text: Let [latex](\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}) \in \mathfrak{R}^{2}[/latex]. The rate of change of the real valued function, [latex]\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})=\mathrm{x}^{2}+\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}^{2}+1[/latex] at the origin in the direction of the point [latex](1,2)[/latex] is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
html:
Let [latex](\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}) \in \mathfrak{R}^{2}[/latex]. The rate of change of the real valued function,

[latex]\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})=\mathrm{x}^{2}+\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}^{2}+1[/latex]

at the origin in the direction of the point [latex](1,2)[/latex] is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
explanation_text:
Step 1: Direction vector and its unit vector The direction vector from origin to point (1, 2) is: [latex] \vec{u} = \langle 1, 2 angle [/latex] Magnitude of this vector is: [latex] |\vec{u}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5} [/latex] Unit vector in the given direction is: [latex] \hat{u} = \left\langle  rac{1}{\sqrt{5}},  rac{2}{\sqrt{5}} ightangle [/latex] Step 2: Compute the gradient of V(x, y) [latex] 
abla V = \left\langle  rac{\partial V}{\partial x},  rac{\partial V}{\partial y} ightangle = \left\langle 2x + 1, 2y ightangle [/latex] At the origin (0, 0), the gradient becomes: [latex] 
abla V(0, 0) = \langle 1, 0 angle [/latex] Step 3: Compute the directional derivative Directional derivative of V in the direction of unit vector [latex] \hat{u} [/latex] is: [latex] D_{\hat{u}} V = 
abla V \cdot \hat{u} = \langle 1, 0 angle \cdot \left\langle  rac{1}{\sqrt{5}},  rac{2}{\sqrt{5}} ightangle =  rac{1}{\sqrt{5}} [/latex] Numerical value: [latex]  rac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \approx  rac{1}{2.236} \approx 0.447 [/latex]
explanation_html:
Step 1: Direction vector and its unit vector
The direction vector from origin to point (1, 2) is:
[latex] \vec{u} = \langle 1, 2 \rangle [/latex]
Magnitude of this vector is:
[latex] |\vec{u}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5} [/latex]
Unit vector in the given direction is:
[latex] \hat{u} = \left\langle \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \right\rangle [/latex]

Step 2: Compute the gradient of V(x, y)
[latex] \nabla V = \left\langle \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \right\rangle = \left\langle 2x + 1, 2y \right\rangle [/latex]
At the origin (0, 0), the gradient becomes:
[latex] \nabla V(0, 0) = \langle 1, 0 \rangle [/latex]

Step 3: Compute the directional derivative
Directional derivative of V in the direction of unit vector [latex] \hat{u} [/latex] is:
[latex] D_{\hat{u}} V = \nabla V \cdot \hat{u} = \langle 1, 0 \rangle \cdot \left\langle \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} [/latex]
Numerical value:
[latex] \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \approx \frac{1}{2.236} \approx 0.447 [/latex]

Let [latex]X [/latex] and [latex]Y [/latex] be continuous random variables with probability density functions [latex]\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{X}}(x)[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{Y}}(y)[/latex], respectively. Further, let [latex]\mathrm{Y}=\mathrm{X}^{2}[/latex] and

[latex] \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{X}}(x)= \begin{cases}1, & x \in (0,1] \\ 0, & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} [/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
explanation_text: Step 1: Given: [latex] Y = X^2 [/latex], and [latex] X \in (0, 1] [/latex] with uniform distribution: [latex] P_X(x) = 1 [/latex] for [latex] x \in (0, 1] [/latex] Step 2: Use the change of variable technique for continuous random variables. If [latex] Y = g(X) = X^2 [/latex], then [latex] X = \sqrt{Y} [/latex] (since [latex] X > 0 [/latex]), and the PDF of [latex] Y [/latex] is: [latex] P_Y(y) = P_X(x) \cdot \left| \frac{dx}{dy} \right| [/latex] We know [latex] x = \sqrt{y} [/latex], so: [latex] \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex] Therefore: [latex] P_Y(y) = P_X(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \left| \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \right| = 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex], for [latex] y \in (0, 1] [/latex] Step 3: So the correct PDF of [latex] Y [/latex] is: [latex] P_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}, & y \in (0, 1] \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} [/latex] Final Answer: (A) [latex] \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex], for [latex] y \in (0, 1] [/latex]
explanation_html:
Step 1: Given: [latex] Y = X^2 [/latex], and [latex] X \in (0, 1] [/latex] with uniform distribution:
[latex] P_X(x) = 1 [/latex] for [latex] x \in (0, 1] [/latex]

Step 2: Use the change of variable technique for continuous random variables.
If [latex] Y = g(X) = X^2 [/latex], then [latex] X = \sqrt{Y} [/latex] (since [latex] X > 0 [/latex]), and the PDF of [latex] Y [/latex] is:
[latex] P_Y(y) = P_X(x) \cdot \left| \frac{dx}{dy} \right| [/latex]
We know [latex] x = \sqrt{y} [/latex], so:
[latex] \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex]
Therefore:
[latex] P_Y(y) = P_X(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \left| \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \right| = 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex], for [latex] y \in (0, 1] [/latex]

Step 3: So the correct PDF of [latex] Y [/latex] is:
[latex] P_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}, & y \in (0, 1] \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} [/latex]

Final Answer: (A) [latex] \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex], for [latex] y \in (0, 1] [/latex]

text: Consider discrete random variables X and Y with probabilities as follows: [latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=0)=\frac{1}{4}[/latex], [latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=0)=\frac{1}{8}[/latex] [latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=1)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] [latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=1)=\frac{1}{8}[/latex] Given [latex]\mathrm{X}=1[/latex], the expected value of [latex]\mathrm{Y}[/latex] is
html:
Consider discrete random variables X and Y with probabilities as follows:

[latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=0)=\frac{1}{4}[/latex],

[latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=0)=\frac{1}{8}[/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=1)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1[/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Y}=1)=\frac{1}{8}[/latex]

Given [latex]\mathrm{X}=1[/latex], the expected value of [latex]\mathrm{Y}[/latex] is
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
explanation_text: Step 1: Identify the conditional probabilities of [latex] Y [/latex] given [latex] X = 1 [/latex]. From the given: [latex] P(X=1, Y=0) = \frac{1}{8}, \quad P(X=1, Y=1) = \frac{1}{8} [/latex] So, total probability [latex] P(X=1) = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{4} [/latex] Step 2: Compute the conditional probabilities: [latex] P(Y=0 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=0)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex] [latex] P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=1)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex] Step 3: Compute the expected value: [latex] \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=1] = 0 \cdot P(Y=0 \mid X=1) + 1 \cdot P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex] Final Answer: (B) [latex] \frac{1}{2} [/latex]
explanation_html:
Step 1: Identify the conditional probabilities of [latex] Y [/latex] given [latex] X = 1 [/latex].
From the given:
[latex] P(X=1, Y=0) = \frac{1}{8}, \quad P(X=1, Y=1) = \frac{1}{8} [/latex]
So, total probability [latex] P(X=1) = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{4} [/latex]

Step 2: Compute the conditional probabilities:
[latex] P(Y=0 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=0)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]
[latex] P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=1)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Step 3: Compute the expected value:
[latex] \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=1] = 0 \cdot P(Y=0 \mid X=1) + 1 \cdot P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Final Answer: (B) [latex] \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

text: Let [latex]v_{1}[/latex] and [latex]v_{2}[/latex] be the two eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues of a [latex]3 \times 3[/latex] real symmetric matrix. Which one of the following statements is true?
html: Let [latex]v_{1}[/latex] and [latex]v_{2}[/latex] be the two eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues of a [latex]3 \times 3[/latex] real symmetric matrix. Which one of the following statements is true?
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
explanation_text: Step 1: Given that the matrix is a real symmetric matrix. Step 3: If [latex] \mathbf{v}_1 [/latex] and [latex] \mathbf{v}_2 [/latex] are eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix, then: [latex] \mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = 0 [/latex] This means they are orthogonal. Step 4: Among the given options, option (B) matches this condition. Final Answer: (B) [latex] \mathbf{v}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = 0 [/latex]

text: Consider the set [latex]S[/latex] of points [latex](x, y) \in  \mathfrak{R}^2[/latex] which minimize the real-valued function [latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex] Which of the following statements is true about the set [latex]S[/latex]?
html:
Consider the set [latex]S[/latex] of points [latex](x, y) \in \mathfrak{R}^2[/latex] which minimize the real-valued function

[latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex]

Which of the following statements is true about the set [latex]S[/latex]?
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
explanation_text: We are given: [latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex] Step 1: Substitute a single variable Let [latex]u = x + y[/latex] Then, the function becomes: [latex]f(x, y) = (u - 1)^2 + u^2 = u^2 - 2u + 1 + u^2 = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex] Step 2: Minimize [latex]f(u) = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex] This is a quadratic function in [latex]u[/latex] with a positive coefficient, so it has a unique minimum. The minimum occurs at: [latex]u = \frac{-(-2)}{2 \cdot 2} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] So, the function is minimized when [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] Step 3: Analyze the set [latex]S[/latex] All points [latex](x, y)[/latex] satisfying [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] will minimize [latex]f(x, y)[/latex]. There are infinitely many such points in [latex]\mathbb{R}^2[/latex]. Final Answer: [latex]\boxed{\text{The number of elements in the set } S \text{ is infinite}}[/latex] Correct Option: (B)
explanation_html:
We are given:
[latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex]

Step 1: Substitute a single variable
Let [latex]u = x + y[/latex]
Then, the function becomes:
[latex]f(x, y) = (u - 1)^2 + u^2 = u^2 - 2u + 1 + u^2 = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex]

Step 2: Minimize [latex]f(u) = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex]
This is a quadratic function in [latex]u[/latex] with a positive coefficient, so it has a unique minimum.
The minimum occurs at:
[latex]u = \frac{-(-2)}{2 \cdot 2} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}[/latex]

So, the function is minimized when [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex]

Step 3: Analyze the set [latex]S[/latex]
All points [latex](x, y)[/latex] satisfying [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] will minimize [latex]f(x, y)[/latex].
There are infinitely many such points in [latex]\mathbb{R}^2[/latex].

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{\text{The number of elements in the set } S \text{ is infinite}}[/latex]
Correct Option: (B)

text: The expected number of trials for first occurrence of a "head" in a biased coin is known to be 4. The probability of first occurrence of a "head" in the second trial is  ___ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
html: The expected number of trials for first occurrence of a "head" in a biased coin is known to be 4. The probability of first occurrence of a "head" in the second trial is ___ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
explanation_html:
Let probability of head [latex]=\mathrm{P}[/latex]
Let probability of Tail [latex]=q=P-1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline Trial & 1 & 2 & 3 & ... \\ \hline Probability & [\mathrm{P} & \mathrm{qP} & [latex]\mathrm{q}^{2} \mathrm{P} & .... \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Expected No. of trail
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p+2 P q+3 q^{2} P+\ldots \\ & =P\left(1+2 q+3 q^{2}+\ldots\right) \\ & =P(1-q)^{-2} \\ & =\frac{P}{P^{2}}=\frac{1}{P} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Given : Trial [latex]=4[/latex]
[latex] \frac{1}{P}=4 \Rightarrow P=\frac{1}{4} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \mathrm{q}=\frac{3}{4}[/latex]

Now, probability of head for second trail. [latex] \begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{qP} \\ & =\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{16}=0.1875 \end{aligned} [/latex]

html:
In the following differential equation, the numerically obtained value of [latex]y(t)[/latex], at [latex]t=1[/latex], is ___ (Round off to 2 decimal places).

[latex] \frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha \mathrm{t}}, \alpha=0.01 \text { and } y(0)=0 [/latex]
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_html:
Given :
[latex] \frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha t} [/latex]
[latex]\alpha=0.01[/latex] and [latex]y(0)=0[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d t^{2}}\right|_{\mathrm{t}=0} & =y^{\prime \prime}(0) \\ & =-\frac{\alpha e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha \mathrm{T}}-\left.\frac{\alpha e^{-\alpha t}}{(2+\alpha \mathrm{t})^{2}}\right|_{\mathrm{t}=0} \\ & =-\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{4}=-\frac{3 \alpha}{4} \end{aligned} [/latex]

We know,
Taylor's series
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(t) & =y(0)+y^{\prime}(0)+\frac{t^{2} y^{\prime \prime}(0)}{2 !}+\ldots \\ & =0+t\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{t^{2}}{2}\left(-\frac{3 \alpha}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{t}{2}-\frac{3}{8} \alpha t^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

At [latex]\mathrm{t}=1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(1) & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{8}(0.01) \times 1^{2} \\ & =0.5-\frac{3}{8} \times 0.01 \\ & =0.496 \approx 0.5 \end{aligned} [/latex]

explanation_text: If two curves cut orthogonally then product of slopes [latex]= -1[/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} x^{2}+y^{2} &=1 \\ 2 x+2 y \frac{d y}{d x} &=0 \\ \left(M_{1}\right)_{u, v} &=\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-x}{y}=\frac{-u}{v} \\ (x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} &=r^{2} \\ \left(M_{2}\right)_{u, v} &=\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=\left(\frac{-2(x-1)}{2(y-1)}\right)_{(u . v)}=\frac{1-u}{v-1} \\ \because \qquad \qquad M_{1} M_{2} &=-1\\ \frac{-u}{v} \times \frac{1-u}{v-1}&=-1\\ -u+u^{2} &=-v^{2}+v \\ u^{2}+v^{2} &=v+u \\ \because \qquad \qquad x^{2}+y^{2} &=1 \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad u+v &=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

text:

of y for [latex]x \in [-2, 0][/latex] are respectively ________
html: The real numbers, x and y with [latex]y = 3x^2 + 3x + 1[/latex], the maximum and minimum value of y for [latex]x \in [-2, 0][/latex] are respectively ________
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
explanation_text:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
y&=3x^{2}+3x+1 \; \;    in \; [-2,0] \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial x}&=6x+3,\; \; \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2}=6  \\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=0\\ 6x+3&=0 \\ x&=\frac{-1}{2} \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{dx^{2}}&=6 \gt 0\text{ minimum} \end{aligned}[/latex] Maximum value of y in [-2, 0] is maximum {f(-2), f(0)} max{7, 1} = 7 Minimum value of y in [-2, 0] [latex]min\begin{Bmatrix} f(-2) & f(0) &f(-\frac{1}{2}) \\ \downarrow, &\downarrow, &\downarrow \\ 7& 1 & \frac{1}{4} \end{Bmatrix}+=\frac{1}{4}[/latex] Maximum value 7, minimum value [latex]\frac{1}{4}[/latex]
explanation_html:

Maximum value of y in [-2, 0] is maximum {f(-2), f(0)}

explanation_text:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=2x-y \\  y(0)&=1, \; y \text{ at } x=\ln  2\\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+y&=2x \\ P&=1, \;\;     Q=2x \\ I.F.&=e^{\int Pdx}=e^{\int 1dx}=e^{x}\\ \text{Solution, }   Y(I.F)&=\int Q(I.F.)dx\\ye^{x}&=\int 2x\cdot e^{x}dx \\&=2(xe^{x}-e^{x})+C \\ y&=2x-2+ce^{-x} \\ y(0)&=1 \\ 1&=0-2+C \\ C&=3 \\ \therefore \; \; y&=2x-2+3e^{-x} \\ \text{At }x&= \ln 2 \\ y&=2(\ln 2)-2+3e^{-\ln 2} \\ &=1.386-2+\frac{3}{2}\\
&=0.886\end{aligned} [/latex]

explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \because \; p& \neq q\\ &\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin p\theta \cos q\theta d\theta \\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} [\sin (p+q)\theta + \sin (p-q)\theta] d\theta \\ &=\frac{1}{4\pi}\left [ \frac{-1}{(p+q)}\cos (p+q)\theta -\frac{1}{(p-q)}\cos (p-q)\theta \right ]_{-\pi}^{\pi}\\ &=\frac{-1}{4\pi} \left \{ \frac{1}{(p+q)}(\cos (p+q) \pi -\cos (p+q)(-\pi)) \right.\\ &+\left. \frac{1}{(p-q)}(\cos (p-q) \pi -\cos (p-q)(-\pi)) \right \}\\ &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

text:

[latex]a \neq 0[/latex]. Which of the following statements is true?
html: [latex]ax^3+bx^2+cx+d[/latex] is a polynomial on real [latex]x[/latex] over real coefficients [latex]a, b, c, d[/latex] wherein [latex]a \neq 0[/latex]. Which of the following statements is true?
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
explanation_text: Given Polynomial [latex]ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0;\; \; \; a\neq 0[/latex] Option (A): If d=0, then the polynomial equation becomes [latex]\begin{aligned} ax^3+bx^2+cx&=0\\ x(ax^2+bx+c)&=0 \\ x=0 \text{ or } ax^2+bx+c&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] d can be choosen to ensure x=0 is a root of given polynomial. Hence, Option (A) is correct. Option B: A third degree polynomial equation with all root equal is given by [latex](x+\alpha )^3=0[/latex] Thus, by selecting suitable values of a, b, c and d we can have all roots identical. Hence, option (B) is incorrect. Option (C): Complex roots always occurs in pairs, So, the given polynomial will have maximum of 2 complex roots and 1 real root. Hence, option (C) is incorrect. Option (D): Nature or roots depends on other coefficients also apart from coefficient 'c'. Hence, option (D) is correct. Hence, the correct options are (A) and (D).
explanation_html:
Given Polynomial [latex]ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0;\; \; \; a\neq 0[/latex]

Option (A):
If d=0, then the polynomial equation becomes
[latex]\begin{aligned} ax^3+bx^2+cx&=0\\ x(ax^2+bx+c)&=0 \\ x=0 \text{ or } ax^2+bx+c&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
d can be choosen to ensure x=0 is a root of given polynomial.
Hence, Option (A) is correct.

Option B:
A third degree polynomial equation with all root equal is given by
[latex](x+\alpha )^3=0[/latex]
Thus, by selecting suitable values of a, b, c and d we can have all roots identical.
Hence, option (B) is incorrect.

Option (C): Complex roots always occurs in pairs,
So, the given polynomial will have maximum of 2 complex roots and 1 real root.
Hence, option (C) is incorrect.

Option (D): Nature or roots depends on other coefficients also apart from coefficient 'c'.
Hence, option (D) is correct.
Hence, the correct options are (A) and (D).

explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} p&=0.02\\ n&=50\\ \lambda &=np=50(0.02)=1\\ p(x\geq 2)&=1-p(x \lt 2)\\ &=1-(p(x=0)+p(x=1))\\ &=1-\left ( \frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^0}{0!}+\frac{e^{-\lambda }\lambda ^1}{1!} \right )\\ &=1-e^{-\lambda }(1+\lambda )\\ &=1-e^{-1}(1+1)=0.26 \end{aligned}[/latex]

explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} f&=2x^3+3y^2+4z\\ \Delta f&=6x^2\hat{i}+6y\hat{j}+4\hat{k}\\ \text{curl} (\Delta f)&=\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x}&\frac{\partial }{\partial y} &\frac{\partial }{\partial z} \\ 6x^2& 6y & 4\end{vmatrix}\\ \therefore \;\;\int _c\Delta f\cdot dr&=\int _c d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)=0\\ &=\int_{(-3,-3,2)}^{2,-3,2}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &+\int_{(2,-3,2)}^{(2,6,2)}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &+\int_{(2,6,2)}^{(2,6,-1)}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &=70+81+(-12)=139 \end{aligned}[/latex]

html: If C is a circle |z|=4 and [latex]f(z)=\frac{z^{2}}{(z^{2}-3z+2)^{2}}[/latex], then [latex]\oint_{C}f(z)dz[/latex] is
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} &\int \frac{z^2}{(z^2-3z+2)^2}dz\\ &\int \frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2}dz\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Res. }f(z)_{z=1}&=\lim_{z \to 1}\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{dz} \left ((z-1)^2\frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 1}\left (\frac{2z(z-2)^2-2z^2(z-2)}{((z-2)^4} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 1}\left (\frac{2z(z-2)-2z^2}{((z-2)^3} \right )=\frac{-4}{-1}=4\\ \text{Res. }f(z)_{z=2}&=\lim_{z \to 2}\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{dz} \left ((z-2)^2\frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 2}\left (\frac{(z-1)^2\cdot 2z-z^22(z-1)}{((z-1)^4} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 2}\left (\frac{2z(z-1)-2z^2}{((z-1)^3} \right )=\frac{4-8}{1}=-4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] By residue theorem, [latex]I=2 \pi i (4-4)=0[/latex]
explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\int \frac{z^2}{(z^2-3z+2)^2}dz\\ &\int \frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2}dz\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Res. }f(z)_{z=1}&=\lim_{z \to 1}\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{dz} \left ((z-1)^2\frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 1}\left (\frac{2z(z-2)^2-2z^2(z-2)}{((z-2)^4} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 1}\left (\frac{2z(z-2)-2z^2}{((z-2)^3} \right )=\frac{-4}{-1}=4\\ \text{Res. }f(z)_{z=2}&=\lim_{z \to 2}\frac{1}{1!}\frac{d}{dz} \left ((z-2)^2\frac{z^2}{(z-1)^2(z-2)^2} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 2}\left (\frac{(z-1)^2\cdot 2z-z^22(z-1)}{((z-1)^4} \right )\\ &=\lim_{z \to 2}\left (\frac{2z(z-1)-2z^2}{((z-1)^3} \right )=\frac{4-8}{1}=-4\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
By residue theorem, [latex]I=2 \pi i (4-4)=0[/latex]

Let f be a real-valued function of a real variable defined as f (x)=x-[x], where [x]
denotes the largest integer less than or equal to x. The value of [latex]\int_{0.25}^{1.25}f(x)dx[/latex] is _______ (up to 2 decimal places).
html: Let f be a real-valued function of a real variable defined as f (x)=x-[x], where [x] denotes the largest integer less than or equal to x. The value of [latex]\int_{0.25}^{1.25}f(x)dx[/latex] is _______ (up to 2 decimal places).
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{0.25}^{1.25} f(x)dx&=\int_{0.25}^{1}(x-[x])dx+\int_{1}^{1.25}(x-[x])dx \\ &= \int_{0.25}^{1.25}(xdx)-\left [ \int_{0.25}^{1}[x]dx+\int_{1}^{1.25}[x]dx \right ]\\ &=\left.\begin{matrix} \left ( \frac{x^2}{2} \right ) \end{matrix}\right|_{0.25}^{1.25}-\left ( \int_{0.25}^{1}0dx+\int_{1}^{1.25}1dx \right ) \\ &=\frac{(1.25)^2}{2}-\left ( \frac{(0.25)^2}{2} \right )-(0+0.25) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}[(1.5625-0.0625)]-0.25 \\ &= 0.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]

text: Consider a non-singular 2x2 square matrix A. If trace(A)=4 and trace([latex]A^{2}[/latex])=5, the determinant of the matrix A is _________(up to 1 decimal place).
html: Consider a non-singular 2x2 square matrix A. If trace(A)=4 and trace([latex]A^{2}[/latex])=5, the determinant of the matrix A is _________(up to 1 decimal place).

explanation_text: A is 2 x 2 matrix [latex]\begin{aligned} Tr\; A&=4\\ \lambda _1+\lambda _2&=4\\ tr(A^2)&=5\\ \lambda _1^2+\lambda _2^2&=5\\ (\lambda _1+\lambda _2)^2&=\lambda _1^2+\lambda _2^2+2\lambda _1 \lambda _2\\ 2\lambda _1 \lambda _2+5&=16\\ 2\lambda _1 \lambda _2&=11\\ \lambda _1 \lambda _2&=\frac{11}{2}\\ |A|&=\frac{11}{2}=5.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]

html: Consider the differential equation [latex](t^{2}-81)\frac{dy}{dt}+5ty=sin(t)[/latex] with [latex] y(1)=2\pi[/latex]. There exists a unique solution for this differential equation when t belongs to the interval
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_text:
The differentail equation, [latex]\begin{aligned}
(t^2-81)\frac{dy}{dt}+5+y&= \sin t\\
\frac{dy}{dt}+\frac{5t}{t^2-81}y&=\frac{\sin t }{t^2-81}\\
P&=\frac{5t}{t^2-81}\\
Q&=\frac{\sin t}{t^2-81}\\
I.F&=e^{\int \rho dt}=e^{\int \frac{5t}{t^2-81}dt}\\
&=e^{\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{2t}{t^2-81}dt}=e^{\frac{5}{2}\ln ({t^2-81})}\\
&=e^{\ln {(t^2-81)^{5/2}}}=(t^2-81)^{5/2}\\

So we need to maximize [latex]\begin{aligned} |A|&=ad-0=ad=a \times -(6+a) \\ &= -a^2-6a\\ \frac{d|A|}{da} &=-2a-6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a &=-3 \text{ is the only stationary point} \end{aligned}[/latex] Since, [latex]\left [\frac{d^2|A|}{da} \right ]_{a=-3}=-2 \lt 0[/latex], we have a maximum at [latex]a=-3[/latex]. text: If a continuous function f(x) does not have a root in the interval [a,b], then which one of the following statements is TRUE?

explanation_text: Intermediate value theorem states that if a function is continious and [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \lt 0[/latex], then surely there is a root in (a,b). The contrapositive of this theorem is that if a function is continious and has no root in (a,b) then surely [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \geq 0[/latex]. But since it is given that there is no root in the closed interval [a,b] it means [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \neq 0[/latex]. So surely [latex]f(a) \cdot f(b) \gt 0[/latex] which is choise(C).

text: A random variable X has probability density function f(x) as given below: [latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix} a+bx & for \; 0 \lt x \lt 1\\ 0& otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] If the expected value E[X]=2/3, then [latex]Pr[X \lt 0.5][/latex] is _____________.
html:
A random variable X has probability density function f(x) as given below:

[latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix} a+bx & for \; 0 \lt x \lt 1\\ 0& otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]

If the expected value E[X]=2/3, then [latex]Pr[X \lt 0.5][/latex] is _____________.
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} a+bx & \text{for }0 \lt x \lt 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{matrix}\right.&\\ \text{Now given }E(X)&=2/3\\ \int_{0}^{1}xf(x)dx&=\frac{2}{3}\\ \int_{0}^{1}x(a+bx)dx&=\frac{2}{3}\\ a\left ( \frac{x^2}{2} \right )_0^1+b\left ( \frac{x^3}{3} \right )_0^1&=\frac{2}{3}\\ a\left ( \frac{1}{2} \right )+b\left ( \frac{1}{3} \right )&=\frac{2}{3}\\ 3a+2b&=4\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Now, }\int_{0}^{1}f(x)dx &=1\\ (\text{total probability} & \text{ is always equal to 1})\\ \int_{0}^{1}(a+bx)dx&=\left ( ax+\frac{bx^2}{2} \right )_0^1=1\\ a+\frac{b}{2}&=1\\ 2a+b&=2\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now solving } & \text{ (i) and (ii), we get}\\ a&=0,b=2\\ So,\; \;f(x)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} 2x & \text{for }0 \lt x lt 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{matrix}\right.&\\ \text{Now we need}&\\ P(x \lt 0.5)&=\int_{0}^{0.5}2xdx=2\left ( \frac{x^2}{2} \right )_0^{0.5}\\ &=0.5^2-0^2=0.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]

text: The function [latex]f(x)=e^{x}-1[/latex] is to be solved using Newton-Raphson method. If the initial value of [latex]x_0[/latex] is taken as 1.0, then the absolute error observed at [latex]2^{nd}[/latex] iteration is _____.
html: The function [latex]f(x)=e^{x}-1[/latex] is to be solved using Newton-Raphson method. If the initial value of [latex]x_0[/latex] is taken as 1.0, then the absolute error observed at [latex]2^{nd}[/latex] iteration is _____.
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Numerical Methods
explanation_text: Given, [latex]f(x)=e^x-1[/latex] or, [latex]f(x_K)=e^{x_K}-1[/latex] and [latex]x_0=1[/latex] In Newton-Raphson method, we have [latex]\begin{aligned} x_{K+1}&=\left [ x_K-\frac{f(x_K)}{f'(x_K)} \right ] \\ x_1&= \left [ x_0- \frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}\right ]\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Now, } f(x_0)&=e^{x_0}-1=e^1-1=(e-1) \\ \text{and, } f'(x)&=e6x \\ \therefore \;\; f'(x_0) &=e^1=e \end{aligned}[/latex] Putting the values, we get: [latex]\begin{aligned} x_1&=\left [ 1-\frac{e-1}{e} \right ]=\left [ \frac{e-e+1}{e} \right ]=e^{-1}\\ \text{Also, }x_2&=\left [ x_1-\frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)} \right ]\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now, }x_1&=\frac{1}{e}=e^{-1} \text{ and } f(x_1)=(e^{e^{-1}}-1)\\ f'(x_1)&=e^{e^{-1}} \end{aligned}[/latex] Putting the value, we get: [latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{e^{-1}}-1)}{e^{e^{-1}}} \right ]\\ &=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{0.37}-1)}{e^{0.37}} \right ]=0.06 \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} v&=\frac{y}{2} \\ dv&=\frac{dy}{2} \\ y=0&= \\ \Rightarrow \;\; v &= 0\\ &y=8 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; v &= 4\\ &\;\;=\int_{0}^{4}\left ( \int_{0}^{1} udu\right )\times 2dv\\ &\;\;= \int_{0}^{4}\left ( \int_{0}^{1} 2udu\right )\times dv \end{aligned}[/latex]

subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
explanation_text: Characteristic equation [latex]|A-\lambda I|=0[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} -\lambda & 1 & -1\\ -6 & -11-\lambda & 6\\ -6&-11 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda [-55+11\lambda -5\lambda +\lambda ^2+66] \\ -1[-30+6\lambda +36]-1[66-66-6\lambda ]=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda (\lambda ^2+6\lambda +11)-1(6\lambda +6)+6\lambda =0 \\ \Rightarrow \;-\lambda ^3-6\lambda ^2-11\lambda -6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda ^3+6\lambda ^2+11\lambda +6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +3)=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda =-1,-2,-3 \end{aligned}[/latex] The absolute values of [latex]\lambda[/latex] are [latex]|\lambda |=1,2,3[/latex] Ratio of maximum and minimum eigen value is [latex]=3:1=\frac{3}{1}=3[/latex]
explanation_html:
Characteristic equation [latex]|A-\lambda I|=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} -\lambda & 1 & -1\\ -6 & -11-\lambda & 6\\ -6&-11 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda [-55+11\lambda -5\lambda +\lambda ^2+66] \\ -1[-30+6\lambda +36]-1[66-66-6\lambda ]=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda (\lambda ^2+6\lambda +11)-1(6\lambda +6)+6\lambda =0 \\ \Rightarrow \;-\lambda ^3-6\lambda ^2-11\lambda -6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda ^3+6\lambda ^2+11\lambda +6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +3)=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda =-1,-2,-3 \end{aligned}[/latex]

text: The line integral of function F=yzi, in the counterclockwise direction, along the circle [latex]x^{2}+y^{2}=1[/latex] at z=1 is
html: The line integral of function F=yzi, in the counterclockwise direction, along the circle [latex]x^{2}+y^{2}=1[/latex] at z=1 is
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \bar{F} &=yz\hat{i} \\ \bigtriangledown \times \bar{F} &=\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x} & \frac{\partial }{\partial y} &\frac{\partial }{\partial z} \\ yz& 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\ &= \hat{i}(0)-\hat{j}(0-y)+\hat{k}(0-z)\\ &=0\hat{i}+y\hat{j}-z\hat{k} \end{aligned}[/latex] By strokes theoram, [latex]\begin{aligned} \int _C\bar{F}\cdot d\bar{r}&=\int _S (\bigtriangledown \times \bar{F})\cdot \hat{n}ds\\ &=\int _S (y\hat{j}-z\hat{k})\cdot \hat{k}ds\\ &=\int _S -z \; ds \;\;\;\text{ Since }\; z=1\\ &=\int _S -1 \; ds=(-1)S=(-1)\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}[/latex] where S is surface area of [latex]x^2+y^2=1[/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;S=\pi(1)^2=\pi[/latex]
explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \bar{F} &=yz\hat{i} \\ \bigtriangledown \times \bar{F} &=\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x} & \frac{\partial }{\partial y} &\frac{\partial }{\partial z} \\ yz& 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\ &= \hat{i}(0)-\hat{j}(0-y)+\hat{k}(0-z)\\ &=0\hat{i}+y\hat{j}-z\hat{k} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By strokes theoram,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \int _C\bar{F}\cdot d\bar{r}&=\int _S (\bigtriangledown \times \bar{F})\cdot \hat{n}ds\\ &=\int _S (y\hat{j}-z\hat{k})\cdot \hat{k}ds\\ &=\int _S -z \; ds \;\;\;\text{ Since }\; z=1\\ &=\int _S -1 \; ds=(-1)S=(-1)\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}[/latex]
where S is surface area of [latex]x^2+y^2=1[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;S=\pi(1)^2=\pi[/latex]

explanation_text: We need absolute maximum of [latex]f(x)=x^3-9x^2+24x+5[/latex] in the interval of [1,6] First find local maximum if any by putting f'(x)=0. [latex]\begin{aligned} f'(x) &=3x^2-18x+24=0 \\ x^2-6x+8&=0 \\ x&=2,4 \\ \text{Now } f''(x) &=6x-18 \\ f''(2)&=12-18=-6 \lt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=2 \text{ is a point of local maximum)} \\ f''(4)&=24-18=+6 \gt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=4 \text{ is a point of local minimum)} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Now tabulate the value of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below [latex]\begin{matrix} x& f(x)\\ 1& 21\\ 2 & 25\\ 6& 41 \end{matrix}[/latex] Clearly the absolute maxima is at x=6 and absolute maximum value is 41.

text: Given that [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 &-3 \\ 2&0 \end{bmatrix} \; and \; I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], the value of [latex]A^{3}[/latex] is
html:
Given that
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 &-3 \\ 2&0 \end{bmatrix} \; and \; I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], the value of [latex]A^{3}[/latex] is
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
explanation_text: [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Characteristic equation of A is [latex]\begin{bmatrix} -5-\lambda & -3\\ 2& 0-\lambda \end{bmatrix}=0[/latex] [latex] (-5-\lambda )(-\lambda )+6=0 [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \lambda ^2+5\lambda +6=0 [/latex] [latex]\text{So,  } A^2+5A+6I=0 [/latex] (by Cayley Hamilton theorem) [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; A^2=-5A-6I [/latex] Multiplying by A on both sides, we have, [latex]A^3=-5A^2-6A[/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow \;\; A^3=-5(-5A-6I)-6A=19A+30I[/latex]
explanation_html:
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Characteristic equation of A is
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -5-\lambda & -3\\ 2& 0-\lambda \end{bmatrix}=0[/latex]
[latex] (-5-\lambda )(-\lambda )+6=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \lambda ^2+5\lambda +6=0 [/latex]
[latex]\text{So, } A^2+5A+6I=0 [/latex]
(by Cayley Hamilton theorem)
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; A^2=-5A-6I [/latex]
Multiplying by A on both sides, we have,
[latex]A^3=-5A^2-6A[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \;\; A^3=-5(-5A-6I)-6A=19A+30I[/latex]

text: With initial condition x(1)=0.5, the solution of the differential equation [latex]t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t[/latex], is
html: With initial condition x(1)=0.5, the solution of the differential equation [latex]t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t[/latex], is
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_text: The given differential equation is [latex]\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(t)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as  [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex] Which is a linear differential equation [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q[/latex] Where,  [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1 Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t[/latex] Solution  is [latex]\begin{aligned} x\cdot (IF) &=\int Q\cdot (IF)dt +C\\ x\cdot t&= \int 1\cdot t\cdot dt+C\\ xt&= \frac{t^2}{2}+C\\ x&= \frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t}\\ \text{Put } x(1)&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; C&=0 \\ \text{So, }x&=\frac{t}{2}\text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]
explanation_html:
The given differential equation is [latex]\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(t)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex]
Which is a linear differential equation
[latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q[/latex]
Where, [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1
Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t[/latex]
Solution is
[latex]\begin{aligned} x\cdot (IF) &=\int Q\cdot (IF)dt +C\\ x\cdot t&= \int 1\cdot t\cdot dt+C\\ xt&= \frac{t^2}{2}+C\\ x&= \frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t}\\ \text{Put } x(1)&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; C&=0 \\ \text{So, }x&=\frac{t}{2}\text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

text: An eigenvector of [latex]P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1&0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0&0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}[/latex] is
html: An eigenvector of [latex]P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1&0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0&0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}[/latex] is
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
explanation_text: Given, [latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 &0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0& 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] P is triangular. So eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves. Eigen values are therefore, [latex]\lambda _1=1,\lambda _2=2,\lambda _3=3.[/latex] Now, the eigen value problem is [latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex] [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1-\lambda &1 &0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 2\\ 0& 0 &3-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Putting [latex]\lambda _1=1[/latex], we get the eigen vector corresponding to this eigen value, [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 0&1 &0 \\ 0 & 1& 2\\ 0& 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Which gives the equations [latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=0 \\ x_2+2x_3&=0 \\ 2x_3 &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] The solution is [latex]x_2=0, x_3=0, x_1=k[/latex] So, one eigen vector is [latex]\hat{x_1}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=k:0:0[/latex] Since, none of the eigen vectors given in choises matches with this, ratio we need to proceed further and find the other eigen vectors corresponding to the other eigen values. Now, corresponding to [latex]\lambda _2=2,[/latex] we get by substituting [latex]\lambda =2,[/latex], in the eigen value problem, the following set of equations, [latex]\begin{bmatrix} -1&1 &0 \\ 0 & 0& 2\\ 0& 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Which gives the equations, [latex]\begin{aligned} -x_1+x_2&=0 \\ 2x_3&=0 \\ x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] Solution is [latex]x_3=0, x_1=k, x_2=k[/latex] [latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_2}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:1:0[/latex] Since none of the eigen vectors given in the choises is of this ratio, we need to proceed further and find 3rd eigen vector also. Which gives the equations,

[latex]\begin{aligned} -2x_1+x_2&=0 \\ -x_2+2x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
putting [latex]x_1=k[/latex], we get, [latex]x_2=2k[/latex] and [latex]x_3=k[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now, } f''(x) &= e^{-x}(2-2x)+(2x-x^2)(-e^{-x})\\ &= e^{-x}(2-2x-(2x-x^2))\\ &= e^{-x}(x^2-4x+2)\\ At\;x=0& \\ f''(0)&= e^{-0}(0-0+2)=2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since [latex]f''(x)=2[/latex] is [latex]\gt 0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex] we have a minima.
Now at [latex]x=2[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} f''(2)&=e^{-2}(2^2-4\times 2 +2) \\ &=-2e^{-2} \lt 0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; At \;\; x=2[/latex] we have a maxima.

text: For the matrix [latex]p=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2&2 \\ 0& -2 & 1\\ 0 &0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] one of the eigen values is equal to -2. Which of the following is an eigen vector ?
html:
For the matrix
[latex]p=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2&2 \\ 0& -2 & 1\\ 0 &0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
one of the eigen values is equal to -2. Which of the following is an eigen vector ?
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
explanation_text:
Since matrix is triangular, the eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves namely [latex]\lambda =3, -2[/latex] and 1. Corresponding to eigen value [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] let us find the eigen vector [latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex] [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 3-\lambda & -2 & 2\\ 0 & -2-\lambda & 1\\ 0& 0 & 1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Putting  [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] in above equation we get, [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ 0& 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Which gives the equations, [latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\\ 3x_3&=0 \;\;...(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex] Since equation (ii) and (iii) are same we have [latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting [latex]x_2=k[/latex], we get [latex]x_3=0, x_2=k[/latex] and [latex]5x_1-2k+2 \times 0=0[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;x_1=2/5 \;k[/latex] Eigen vectors are of the form [latex]\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2/5 k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} x_1:x_2:x_3&=2/5k:k:0\\ &=2/5:1:0\\ &=2:5:0 \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 5\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is an eigen vector of matrix p.

Since matrix is triangular, the eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves namely [latex]\lambda =3, -2[/latex] and 1.
Corresponding to eigen value [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] let us find the eigen vector
[latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 3-\lambda & -2 & 2\\ 0 & -2-\lambda & 1\\ 0& 0 & 1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Putting [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] in above equation we get,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ 0& 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations,
[latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\\ 3x_3&=0 \;\;...(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since equation (ii) and (iii) are same we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}[/latex] Putting [latex]x_2=k[/latex], we get
[latex]x_3=0, x_2=k[/latex] and [latex]5x_1-2k+2 \times 0=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;x_1=2/5 \;k[/latex]
Eigen vectors are of the form

[latex]\begin{aligned} x_1:x_2:x_3&=2/5k:k:0\\ &=2/5:1:0\\ &=2:5:0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 5\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is an eigen vector of matrix p.

text: Let [latex]y[/latex] be the solution of the differential equation with the initial conditions given below. If [latex]y(x=2)=A \ln 2[/latex], then the value of [latex]A[/latex] is __________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places). [latex] x^{2}\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+3x\frac{dy}{dx}+y=0, \quad y(x=1)=0, \quad \frac{dy}{dx}(x=1)=1 [/latex]
html:
Let [latex]y[/latex] be the solution of the differential equation with the initial conditions given below. If [latex]y(x=2)=A \ln 2[/latex], then the value of [latex]A[/latex] is __________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).

[latex] x^{2}\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+3x\frac{dy}{dx}+y=0, \quad y(x=1)=0, \quad \frac{dy}{dx}(x=1)=1 [/latex]
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_text: Given: [latex] x^2 \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 3x \frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0 [/latex] Initial conditions: [latex] y(1) = 0, \quad \frac{dy}{dx}(1) = 1 [/latex] It is also given that [latex] y(2) = A \ln 2 [/latex], find [latex] A [/latex]. Step 1: Identify the type of differential equation This is a Cauchy-Euler equation of the form: [latex] x^2 y'' + ax y' + b y = 0 [/latex] Here, [latex] a = 3, \quad b = 1 [/latex] Step 2: Use the substitution Let [latex] x = e^t \Rightarrow t = \ln x [/latex], and define [latex] y(x) = u(t) [/latex] Then: [latex] \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{du}{dt} [/latex] [latex] \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{x^2} \cdot \left( \frac{d^2u}{dt^2} - \frac{du}{dt} \right) [/latex] Substituting into the original equation: [latex] x^2 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{x^2} \left( \frac{d^2u}{dt^2} - \frac{du}{dt} \right) \right) + 3x \cdot \left( \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{du}{dt} \right) + u = 0 [/latex] Simplifying: [latex] \frac{d^2u}{dt^2} - \frac{du}{dt} + 3 \frac{du}{dt} + u = 0 [/latex] [latex] \frac{d^2u}{dt^2} + 2 \frac{du}{dt} + u = 0 [/latex] Step 3: Solve the transformed equation [latex] u'' + 2u' + u = 0 [/latex] Auxiliary equation: [latex] r^2 + 2r + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow (r + 1)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow r = -1 [/latex] (repeated root) So, general solution: [latex] u(t) = (A + Bt)e^{-t} [/latex] Step 4: Convert back to [latex] y(x) [/latex] Since [latex] t = \ln x [/latex], [latex] y(x) = u(\ln x) = (A + B \ln x) \cdot x^{-1} = \frac{A + B \ln x}{x} [/latex] Step 5: Apply initial conditions [latex] y(1) = \frac{A + B \ln 1}{1} = A = 0 [/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow A = 0 [/latex] Now differentiate: [latex] y(x) = \frac{B \ln x}{x} [/latex] [latex] y'(x) = B \cdot \left( \frac{1 - \ln x}{x^2} \right) [/latex] At [latex] x = 1 [/latex]: [latex] y'(1) = B(1 - \ln 1) = B(1) = B [/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow B = 1 [/latex] Step 6: Evaluate [latex] y(2) [/latex] [latex] y(x) = \frac{\ln x}{x} [/latex] [latex] y(2) = \frac{\ln 2}{2} [/latex] Given [latex] y(2) = A \ln 2 [/latex], So, [latex] A \ln 2 = \frac{\ln 2}{2} \Rightarrow A = \frac{1}{2} = 0.50 [/latex] Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{0.50} [/latex] (rounded off to 2 decimal places)
explanation_html:
Given:
[latex] x^2 \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 3x \frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0 [/latex]
Initial conditions: [latex] y(1) = 0, \quad \frac{dy}{dx}(1) = 1 [/latex]
It is also given that [latex] y(2) = A \ln 2 [/latex], find [latex] A [/latex].

Step 1: Identify the type of differential equation
This is a Cauchy-Euler equation of the form:
[latex] x^2 y'' + ax y' + b y = 0 [/latex]
Here, [latex] a = 3, \quad b = 1 [/latex]

Step 2: Use the substitution
Let [latex] x = e^t \Rightarrow t = \ln x [/latex], and define [latex] y(x) = u(t) [/latex]
Then:
[latex] \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{du}{dt} [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{x^2} \cdot \left( \frac{d^2u}{dt^2} - \frac{du}{dt} \right) [/latex]

Substituting into the original equation:
[latex] x^2 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{x^2} \left( \frac{d^2u}{dt^2} - \frac{du}{dt} \right) \right) + 3x \cdot \left( \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{du}{dt} \right) + u = 0 [/latex]
Simplifying:
[latex] \frac{d^2u}{dt^2} - \frac{du}{dt} + 3 \frac{du}{dt} + u = 0 [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d^2u}{dt^2} + 2 \frac{du}{dt} + u = 0 [/latex]

Step 3: Solve the transformed equation
[latex] u'' + 2u' + u = 0 [/latex]
Auxiliary equation: [latex] r^2 + 2r + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow (r + 1)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow r = -1 [/latex] (repeated root)
So, general solution:
[latex] u(t) = (A + Bt)e^{-t} [/latex]

Step 4: Convert back to [latex] y(x) [/latex]
Since [latex] t = \ln x [/latex],
[latex] y(x) = u(\ln x) = (A + B \ln x) \cdot x^{-1} = \frac{A + B \ln x}{x} [/latex]

Step 5: Apply initial conditions
[latex] y(1) = \frac{A + B \ln 1}{1} = A = 0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow A = 0 [/latex]

Now differentiate:
[latex] y(x) = \frac{B \ln x}{x} [/latex]
[latex] y'(x) = B \cdot \left( \frac{1 - \ln x}{x^2} \right) [/latex]
At [latex] x = 1 [/latex]:
[latex] y'(1) = B(1 - \ln 1) = B(1) = B [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow B = 1 [/latex]

Step 6: Evaluate [latex] y(2) [/latex]
[latex] y(x) = \frac{\ln x}{x} [/latex]
[latex] y(2) = \frac{\ln 2}{2} [/latex]

Given [latex] y(2) = A \ln 2 [/latex],
So, [latex] A \ln 2 = \frac{\ln 2}{2} \Rightarrow A = \frac{1}{2} = 0.50 [/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex] \boxed{0.50} [/latex] (rounded off to 2 decimal places)

explanation_html:
Given:
Function: [latex] f(x, y) = x^2 + x y^2 [/latex]
Point: [latex] (1, 0) [/latex]
Direction: [latex] \frac{1}{2}(\hat{i} + \sqrt{3} \hat{j}) [/latex]

Step 1: Find the gradient of [latex]f[/latex]
[latex] \nabla f = \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right) [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2x + y^2 [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2xy [/latex]

At point [latex] (1, 0) [/latex]:
[latex] \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2(1) + 0^2 = 2 [/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2(1)(0) = 0 [/latex]
So, [latex] \nabla f(1, 0) = (2, 0) [/latex]

Step 2: Unit direction vector
Given vector: [latex] \vec{v} = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{i} + \sqrt{3} \hat{j}) [/latex]
Magnitude of [latex] \vec{v} [/latex]:
[latex] \left| \vec{v} \right| = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{1^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{1 + 3} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 = 1 [/latex]
So the given vector is already a unit vector: [latex] \hat{u} = \left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) [/latex]

Step 3: Directional derivative
[latex] D_{\hat{u}} f = \nabla f \cdot \hat{u} = (2, 0) \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 0 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 1 [/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex] \boxed{1.0} [/latex] (rounded off to 1 decimal place)

text: If [latex]C[/latex] is the unit circle in the complex plane with its center at the origin, then the value of [latex]n[/latex] in the equation given below is __________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place). [latex] \oint_{c}\frac{z^{3}}{(z^{2}+4)(z^{2}-4)}dz=2 \pi i n [/latex]
html:
If [latex]C[/latex] is the unit circle in the complex plane with its center at the origin, then the value of [latex]n[/latex] in the equation given below is __________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).

[latex] \oint_{c}\frac{z^{3}}{(z^{2}+4)(z^{2}-4)}dz=2 \pi i n [/latex]
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
explanation_text: Given: [latex] C [/latex] is the unit circle centered at the origin in the complex plane. We are given the integral: [latex] \oint_C \frac{z^3}{(z^2 + 4)(z^2 - 4)} , dz = 2\pi i n [/latex] We are to find the value of [latex] n [/latex]. Step 1: Simplify the denominator [latex] (z^2 + 4)(z^2 - 4) = (z^2 + 4)(z - 2)(z + 2) [/latex] So the integrand becomes: [latex] \frac{z^3}{(z - 2)(z + 2)(z^2 + 4)} [/latex] Step 2: Identify singularities (poles) Poles of the function are at: [latex] z = 2, \quad z = -2, \quad z = 2i, \quad z = -2i [/latex] Step 3: Determine which poles lie inside the unit circle The unit circle is [latex] |z| = 1 [/latex]. All poles lie outside the unit circle because: [latex] |2| = 2 > 1,\quad |-2| = 2 > 1,\quad |2i| = 2 > 1,\quad |-2i| = 2 > 1 [/latex] So, there are no poles inside the contour. Step 4: Apply Cauchy's Theorem Since the integrand is analytic inside and on the contour, the integral is zero: [latex] \oint_C \frac{z^3}{(z^2 + 4)(z^2 - 4)} , dz = 0 [/latex] Compare with the given expression: [latex] 2\pi i n = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n = 0 [/latex] Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{n = 0.0} [/latex]
explanation_html:
Given:
[latex] C [/latex] is the unit circle centered at the origin in the complex plane.
We are given the integral:
[latex] \oint_C \frac{z^3}{(z^2 + 4)(z^2 - 4)} , dz = 2\pi i n [/latex]
We are to find the value of [latex] n [/latex].

Step 1: Simplify the denominator
[latex] (z^2 + 4)(z^2 - 4) = (z^2 + 4)(z - 2)(z + 2) [/latex]

So the integrand becomes:
[latex] \frac{z^3}{(z - 2)(z + 2)(z^2 + 4)} [/latex]

Step 2: Identify singularities (poles)
Poles of the function are at:
[latex] z = 2, \quad z = -2, \quad z = 2i, \quad z = -2i [/latex]

Step 3: Determine which poles lie inside the unit circle
The unit circle is [latex] |z| = 1 [/latex].
All poles lie outside the unit circle because:
[latex] |2| = 2 > 1,\quad |-2| = 2 > 1,\quad |2i| = 2 > 1,\quad |-2i| = 2 > 1 [/latex]
So, there are no poles inside the contour.

Step 4: Apply Cauchy's Theorem
Since the integrand is analytic inside and on the contour, the integral is zero:
[latex] \oint_C \frac{z^3}{(z^2 + 4)(z^2 - 4)} , dz = 0 [/latex]

Compare with the given expression:
[latex] 2\pi i n = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n = 0 [/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex] \boxed{n = 0.0} [/latex]

text: In the closed interval [0, 3], the minimum value of the function [latex]f[/latex] given below is [latex]f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x [/latex]
html:
In the closed interval [0, 3], the minimum value of the function [latex]f[/latex] given below is

[latex]f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x [/latex]
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_text:
Given: [latex]f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x[/latex] over the closed interval [0, 3] Step 1: Find the derivative [latex]f'(x)[/latex] to get critical points [latex]f'(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}(2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x) = 6x^2 - 18x + 12[/latex] Step 2: Set [latex]f'(x) = 0[/latex] and solve for [latex]x[/latex] [latex]6x^2 - 18x + 12 = 0[/latex]
Divide entire equation by 6: [latex]x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0[/latex] [latex](x - 1)(x - 2) = 0[/latex] So, critical points are [latex]x = 1[/latex] and [latex]x = 2[/latex] Step 3: Evaluate [latex]f(x)[/latex] at endpoints and critical points [latex]f(0) = 2(0)^3 - 9(0)^2 + 12(0) = 0[/latex] [latex]f(1) = 2(1)^3 - 9(1)^2 + 12(1) = 2 - 9 + 12 = 5[/latex] [latex]f(2) = 2(8) - 9(4) + 12(2) = 16 - 36 + 24 = 4[/latex] [latex]f(3) = 2(27) - 9(9) + 12(3) = 54 - 81 + 36 = 9[/latex] Step 4: Find the minimum value among these [latex]\min{0,\ 4,\ 5,\ 9} = 0[/latex]
explanation_html:
Given:
[latex]f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x[/latex] over the closed interval [0, 3]

Step 1: Find the derivative [latex]f'(x)[/latex] to get critical points
[latex]f'(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}(2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x) = 6x^2 - 18x + 12[/latex]

Step 2: Set [latex]f'(x) = 0[/latex] and solve for [latex]x[/latex]
[latex]6x^2 - 18x + 12 = 0[/latex] Divide entire equation by 6:
[latex]x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0[/latex]
[latex](x - 1)(x - 2) = 0[/latex]
So, critical points are [latex]x = 1[/latex] and [latex]x = 2[/latex]

Step 3: Evaluate [latex]f(x)[/latex] at endpoints and critical points
[latex]f(0) = 2(0)^3 - 9(0)^2 + 12(0) = 0[/latex]
[latex]f(1) = 2(1)^3 - 9(1)^2 + 12(1) = 2 - 9 + 12 = 5[/latex]
[latex]f(2) = 2(8) - 9(4) + 12(2) = 16 - 36 + 24 = 4[/latex]
[latex]f(3) = 2(27) - 9(9) + 12(3) = 54 - 81 + 36 = 9[/latex]

Step 4: Find the minimum value among these
[latex]\min{0,\ 4,\ 5,\ 9} = 0[/latex]

Using Simpson's one-third rule,

subject: Engineering Mathematics - Numerical Methods
explanation_text:
Given: The values of the function [latex] f(x) [/latex] at different [latex] x [/latex] are:
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 0.25 & 0.5 & 0.75 & 1.0 \\ \hline f(x) & 0.9 & 2.0 & 1.5 & 1.8 & 0.4 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex] We will apply Simpson’s 1/3 Rule: [latex] \int_{a}^{b} f(x), dx \approx \frac{h}{3} \left[ f(x_0) + 4(f(x_1) + f(x_3)) + 2(f(x_2)) + f(x_4) \right] [/latex] Here, [latex] h = \frac{1 - 0}{4} = 0.25 [/latex] Substituting values: [latex] \int_0^1 f(x),dx \approx \frac{0.25}{3} \left[ 0.9 + 4(2.0 + 1.8) + 2(1.5) + 0.4 \right] [/latex] [latex] = \frac{0.25}{3} \left[ 0.9 + 4(3.8) + 3.0 + 0.4 \right] [/latex] [latex] = \frac{0.25}{3} \times (0.9 + 15.2 + 3.0 + 0.4) = \frac{0.25}{3} \times 19.5 [/latex] [latex] = \frac{4.875}{3} = 1.625 [/latex] Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{1.63} [/latex] (rounded to 2 decimal places)
explanation_html:
Given:
The values of the function [latex] f(x) [/latex] at different [latex] x [/latex] are: [latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & 0.25 & 0.5 & 0.75 & 1.0 \\ \hline f(x) & 0.9 & 2.0 & 1.5 & 1.8 & 0.4 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

We will apply Simpson’s 1/3 Rule:
[latex] \int_{a}^{b} f(x), dx \approx \frac{h}{3} \left[ f(x_0) + 4(f(x_1) + f(x_3)) + 2(f(x_2)) + f(x_4) \right] [/latex]

Here, [latex] h = \frac{1 - 0}{4} = 0.25 [/latex]

Substituting values:
[latex] \int_0^1 f(x),dx \approx \frac{0.25}{3} \left[ 0.9 + 4(2.0 + 1.8) + 2(1.5) + 0.4 \right] [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{0.25}{3} \left[ 0.9 + 4(3.8) + 3.0 + 0.4 \right] [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{0.25}{3} \times (0.9 + 15.2 + 3.0 + 0.4) = \frac{0.25}{3} \times 19.5 [/latex]
[latex] = \frac{4.875}{3} = 1.625 [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{1.63} [/latex] (rounded to 2 decimal places)

text: If two unbiased coins are tossed, then what is the probability of having at least one head?
html: If two unbiased coins are tossed, then what is the probability of having at least one head?
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
explanation_text: Given: Two unbiased coins are tossed. Step 1: Identifying the Sample Space When two unbiased coins are tossed, the possible outcomes are: [latex] {HH, HT, TH, TT} [/latex] Thus, the total number of possible outcomes is 4. Step 2: Counting Favorable Outcomes The event "at least one head" includes the outcomes: [latex] {HH, HT, TH} [/latex] The number of favorable outcomes = 3. Step 3: Computing the Probability Probability formula: [latex] P(\text{at least one head}) = \frac{\text{Number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total outcomes}} [/latex] [latex] P = \frac{3}{4} = 0.75 [/latex]
explanation_html:
Given: Two unbiased coins are tossed.

Step 1: Identifying the Sample Space
When two unbiased coins are tossed, the possible outcomes are:
[latex] {HH, HT, TH, TT} [/latex]
Thus, the total number of possible outcomes is 4.

Step 2: Counting Favorable Outcomes
The event "at least one head" includes the outcomes:
[latex] {HH, HT, TH} [/latex]
The number of favorable outcomes = 3.

Step 3: Computing the Probability
Probability formula:
[latex] P(\text{at least one head}) = \frac{\text{Number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total outcomes}} [/latex]
[latex] P = \frac{3}{4} = 0.75 [/latex]

subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_text:
Given: The differential equation: [latex]  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0 [/latex] for [latex] 0 \leq x \leq 1, 0 \leq y \leq 1 [/latex]. Step 1: Understanding the Given Equation The given equation is the Laplace equation in two variables. A function [latex] u(x, y) [/latex] is a solution if its second partial derivatives sum to zero: [latex]  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0 [/latex]. Step 2: Checking Each Option Option (A): [latex] u = e^{x+y} [/latex] First derivative: [latex]  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} = e^{x+y}, \quad  rac{\partial u}{\partial y} = e^{x+y} [/latex] Second derivative: [latex]  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = e^{x+y}, \quad  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = e^{x+y} [/latex] Summing them: [latex] e^{x+y} + e^{x+y} = 2e^{x+y} 
eq 0 [/latex] This is not a solution. Option (B): [latex] u = e^x \sin y [/latex] First derivatives: [latex]  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} = e^x \sin y, \quad  rac{\partial u}{\partial y} = e^x \cos y [/latex] Second derivatives: [latex]  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = e^x \sin y, \quad  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -e^x \sin y [/latex] Summing them: [latex] e^x \sin y - e^x \sin y = 0 [/latex] This is a valid solution. ✅ Option (C): [latex] u = \sin x \sin y [/latex] First derivatives: [latex]  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \cos x \sin y, \quad  rac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \sin x \cos y [/latex] Second derivatives: [latex]  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = -\sin x \sin y, \quad  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -\sin x \sin y [/latex] Summing them: [latex] -\sin x \sin y - \sin x \sin y = -2\sin x \sin y 
eq 0 [/latex] This is not a solution. Option (D): [latex] u = \cos x \cos y [/latex] First derivatives: [latex]  rac{\partial u}{\partial x} = -\sin x \cos y, \quad  rac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\cos x \sin y [/latex] Second derivatives: [latex]  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = -\cos x \cos y, \quad  rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -\cos x \cos y [/latex] Summing them: [latex] -\cos x \cos y - \cos x \cos y = -2\cos x \cos y 
eq 0 [/latex] This is not a solution. Final Answer: The correct option is: [latex]  oxed{u = e^x \sin y} [/latex] ✅
explanation_html:
Given: The differential equation:
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0 [/latex] for [latex] 0 \leq x \leq 1, 0 \leq y \leq 1 [/latex].

Step 1: Understanding the Given Equation
The given equation is the Laplace equation in two variables.
A function [latex] u(x, y) [/latex] is a solution if its second partial derivatives sum to zero:
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0 [/latex].

Step 2: Checking Each Option
Option (A): [latex] u = e^{x+y} [/latex]
First derivative:
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = e^{x+y}, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = e^{x+y} [/latex]
Second derivative:
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = e^{x+y}, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = e^{x+y} [/latex]
Summing them:
[latex] e^{x+y} + e^{x+y} = 2e^{x+y} \neq 0 [/latex]
This is not a solution.

Option (B): [latex] u = e^x \sin y [/latex]
First derivatives:
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = e^x \sin y, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = e^x \cos y [/latex]
Second derivatives:
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = e^x \sin y, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -e^x \sin y [/latex]
Summing them:
[latex] e^x \sin y - e^x \sin y = 0 [/latex]
This is a valid solution. ✅

Option (C): [latex] u = \sin x \sin y [/latex]
First derivatives:
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \cos x \sin y, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \sin x \cos y [/latex]
Second derivatives:
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = -\sin x \sin y, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -\sin x \sin y [/latex]
Summing them:
[latex] -\sin x \sin y - \sin x \sin y = -2\sin x \sin y \neq 0 [/latex]
This is not a solution.

Option (D): [latex] u = \cos x \cos y [/latex]
First derivatives:
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = -\sin x \cos y, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\cos x \sin y [/latex]
Second derivatives:
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = -\cos x \cos y, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = -\cos x \cos y [/latex]
Summing them:
[latex] -\cos x \cos y - \cos x \cos y = -2\cos x \cos y \neq 0 [/latex]
This is not a solution.

Final Answer:
The correct option is:
[latex] \boxed{u = e^x \sin y} [/latex] ✅

text: Let [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] be real symmetric matrices of same size. Which one of the following options is correct?
html: Let [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] be real symmetric matrices of same size. Which one of the following options is correct?
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
explanation_text:
Given: [latex] A [/latex] and [latex] B [/latex] are real symmetric matrices of the same size. Step 1: Understanding Symmetric Matrices A matrix [latex] A [/latex] is symmetric if: [latex] A^T = A [/latex] Similarly, [latex] B [/latex] is symmetric if: [latex] B^T = B [/latex] This property will help us evaluate the given options. Step 2: Evaluating the Given Options Option (A): [latex] A^T = A^{-1} [/latex] - This statement says that the transpose of [latex] A [/latex] is its inverse.
- In general, a symmetric matrix [latex] A [/latex] satisfies [latex] A^T = A [/latex], but there is no guarantee that [latex] A^T = A^{-1} [/latex].
- This is true only if [latex] A [/latex] is an **orthogonal matrix**, which is not given in the problem.
- Thus, this statement is incorrect. Option (B): [latex] AB = BA [/latex] - In general, two symmetric matrices **do not necessarily commute**.
- That is, [latex] AB \neq BA [/latex] in most cases.
- Thus, this statement is incorrect. Option (C): [latex] (AB)^T = B^T A^T [/latex] - Using the property of transposition:  
  [latex] (AB)^T = B^T A^T [/latex] - Since [latex] A [/latex] and [latex] B [/latex] are symmetric, we substitute [latex] A^T = A [/latex] and [latex] B^T = B [/latex]:  
  [latex] (AB)^T = B A [/latex] - This matches the given statement.
- Thus, this statement is correct. ✅ Option (D): [latex] A = A^{-1} [/latex] - A matrix satisfying [latex] A = A^{-1} [/latex] is called an **involutory matrix**.
- However, not all symmetric matrices satisfy this property.
- The problem does not state that [latex] A [/latex] is involutory.
- Thus, this statement is incorrect. Final Answer: The correct option is: [latex] \boxed{(AB)^T = B^T A^T} [/latex]
explanation_html:
Given: [latex] A [/latex] and [latex] B [/latex] are real symmetric matrices of the same size.

Step 1: Understanding Symmetric Matrices
A matrix [latex] A [/latex] is symmetric if:
[latex] A^T = A [/latex]
Similarly, [latex] B [/latex] is symmetric if:
[latex] B^T = B [/latex]
This property will help us evaluate the given options.

Step 2: Evaluating the Given Options
Option (A): [latex] A^T = A^{-1} [/latex]
- This statement says that the transpose of [latex] A [/latex] is its inverse. - In general, a symmetric matrix [latex] A [/latex] satisfies [latex] A^T = A [/latex], but there is no guarantee that [latex] A^T = A^{-1} [/latex]. - This is true only if [latex] A [/latex] is an **orthogonal matrix**, which is not given in the problem. - Thus, this statement is incorrect.

Option (B): [latex] AB = BA [/latex]
- In general, two symmetric matrices **do not necessarily commute**. - That is, [latex] AB \neq BA [/latex] in most cases. - Thus, this statement is incorrect.

Option (C): [latex] (AB)^T = B^T A^T [/latex]
- Using the property of transposition: [latex] (AB)^T = B^T A^T [/latex]
- Since [latex] A [/latex] and [latex] B [/latex] are symmetric, we substitute [latex] A^T = A [/latex] and [latex] B^T = B [/latex]: [latex] (AB)^T = B A [/latex]
- This matches the given statement. - Thus, this statement is correct. ✅

Option (D): [latex] A = A^{-1} [/latex]
- A matrix satisfying [latex] A = A^{-1} [/latex] is called an **involutory matrix**. - However, not all symmetric matrices satisfy this property. - The problem does not state that [latex] A [/latex] is involutory. - Thus, this statement is incorrect.

Final Answer:
The correct option is:
[latex] \boxed{(AB)^T = B^T A^T} [/latex]

text: Let [latex]f(z)[/latex] be an analytic function, where [latex]z=x+i y[/latex]. If the real part of [latex]f(z)[/latex] is [latex]\cosh x \cos y[/latex], and the imaginary part of [latex]f(z)[/latex] is zero for [latex]y=0[/latex], then [latex]f(z)[/latex] is

subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
explanation_html:
The necessary and sufficient condition for a function [latex]f(z)=u(x, y)+i v(x, y)[/latex] to be analytic is it should satisfy the cauchy Riemann equation.

C.R. equation:
[latex] \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \quad \text { or, } \quad u_{x}=v_{y} [/latex]
[latex]\&, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}[/latex] or, [latex]u_{y}=-v_{x}[/latex]
Given: [latex]\quad \mathrm{u}=\cosh \mathrm{x} \cos y[/latex]
Now, [latex]\quad u_{x}=\sinh x \cos y[/latex]
and, [latex]\quad u_{y}=-\cosh x \sin y[/latex]

To find [latex]f(z)[/latex], put [latex]x=z \& y=0[/latex];
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(z)&=\int\left(u_{x}-i u_{y}\right) d z \\ &=\int[\sinh z \cdot \cos 0-(-\cosh z \cdot \sin 0)] d z \\ &=\int \sinh z d z=\cosh z+C \end{aligned} [/latex]

html:
In order to numerically solve the ordinary differential equation [latex]\frac{d y}{d t}=-y[/latex] for [latex]t > 0[/latex], with an initial condition [latex]y(0)=1[/latex], the following scheme is employed

[latex]\frac{\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}+1}-\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}-1}+\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}\right)[/latex]

Here, [latex]\Delta t[/latex] is the time step and [latex]y_{n}=y(n \Delta t)[/latex] for [latex]n[/latex] [latex]=0,1,2, \ldots[/latex] Thus numerical scheme will yield a solution with non-physical oscillations for [latex]\Delta \mathrm{t} > \mathrm{h}[/latex]. The value of [latex]\mathrm{h}[/latex] is
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_text:
Given, [latex]
\begin{aligned}
\frac{y_{n+1}-y_n}{\Delta t} & =\frac{1}{2}\left(y_{n+1}+y_n\right) \\
y_{n+1}-y_n & =\frac{\Delta t}{2}\left(y_{n+1}+y_n\right) \\
y_{n+1}-\frac{\Delta t}{2} y_{n+1} & =y_n+\frac{\Delta t}{2} y_n \\
y_{n+1} & =\frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t} y_n
\end{aligned}
[/latex] For stability or non physical oscillations, [latex]
\begin{aligned}
\left|\frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t}\right| & \leq 1 \\
-1 & \leq \frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t} \leq 1 \\
-1 & \leq-1+\frac{4}{2-\Delta t} \leq 1 \\
0 & \leq \frac{4}{2-\Delta t} \leq 2 \\
\frac{1}{2} & \leq \frac{2-\Delta t}{4} \leq 0 \\
2 & \leq 2-\Delta t \leq 0 \\
0 & \leq-\Delta t \leq-2 \\
\Delta t & \geq 2
\end{aligned}
[/latex] [latex]
\therefore \quad \Delta t \geq 2
[/latex] Thus from given options, option (D) is correct.
explanation_html:
Given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{y_{n+1}-y_n}{\Delta t} & =\frac{1}{2}\left(y_{n+1}+y_n\right) \\ y_{n+1}-y_n & =\frac{\Delta t}{2}\left(y_{n+1}+y_n\right) \\ y_{n+1}-\frac{\Delta t}{2} y_{n+1} & =y_n+\frac{\Delta t}{2} y_n \\ y_{n+1} & =\frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t} y_n \end{aligned} [/latex]
For stability or non physical oscillations,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left|\frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t}\right| & \leq 1 \\ -1 & \leq \frac{2+\Delta t}{2-\Delta t} \leq 1 \\ -1 & \leq-1+\frac{4}{2-\Delta t} \leq 1 \\ 0 & \leq \frac{4}{2-\Delta t} \leq 2 \\ \frac{1}{2} & \leq \frac{2-\Delta t}{4} \leq 0 \\ 2 & \leq 2-\Delta t \leq 0 \\ 0 & \leq-\Delta t \leq-2 \\ \Delta t & \geq 2 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \Delta t \geq 2 [/latex]
Thus from given options, option (D) is correct.

explanation_text:
Solution of differential equation given by forward Euler's method is [latex]
y_{n+1}=y_{n}+h f\left(x_{n}, y_{n}\right)
[/latex] Given: [latex]\frac{d y}{d t}+2 y=0[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d t}=-2 y[/latex] and step size, [latex]\mathrm{h}=\Delta \mathrm{t}[/latex] [latex]\therefore \quad y_{n+1}=y_{n}+\Delta t\left(-2 y_{n}\right)[/latex] [latex]\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}+1}=\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}(1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t})[/latex] [latex]\frac{y_{n+1}}{y_{n}}=1-2 \Delta t \;\;\;...(i)[/latex] Given: [latex]

\Delta t \geq 0

1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t} \geq-1
[/latex] [latex]
\Delta \mathrm{t} \leq 1
[/latex] [latex]\therefore \quad[/latex] Value of [latex]\Delta t: 0 \leq \Delta t \leq 1[/latex]
explanation_html:
Solution of differential equation given by forward Euler's method is
[latex] y_{n+1}=y_{n}+h f\left(x_{n}, y_{n}\right) [/latex]
Given: [latex]\frac{d y}{d t}+2 y=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d t}=-2 y[/latex]
and step size, [latex]\mathrm{h}=\Delta \mathrm{t}[/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}+1}=\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{n}}(1-2 \Delta \mathrm{t})[/latex]

Then, [latex]\quad 1-2 \Delta t \leq 1[/latex]

then [latex]-(1-2 \Delta t) \leq 1[/latex]

html:
Consider the second-order linear ordinary differential equation

[latex]x^2\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}+x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=0,\;\; x \geq 1[/latex]

with the initial conditions

[latex]y(x=1)=6,\;\;\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{dy}{dx} \end{matrix}\right|_{x=1}=2[/latex]

The value of [latex]y[/latex] at [latex]x=2[/latex] equals _________. (Answer in integer)
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_text:
[latex]
\frac{x d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+\frac{x d y}{d x}-y=0, x \geq 1
[/latex] This is an Euler-cauchy equation and has solutions of the form [latex]
\begin{aligned}
& y=x^{n} \\
& y^{\prime}=n x^{n-1} \\
& y^{\prime \prime}=n(n-1) x^{n-2} \\
& x^{2}(n)(n-1) x^{n-2}+x\left(n x^{n-1}\right)-x^{n}=0 \\
& x^{n}[x(n-1)+n-1)=0 \\
& n^{2}-1=0 \\
& n=\pm 1 \\
& y_{1}=x \\
& y_{2}=\frac{1}{x} \\
& y=C_{1} x+\frac{C_{2}}{x}
\end{aligned}
[/latex] Given [latex]y(x=1)=6[/latex] [latex]
\begin{aligned}
6 & =C_{1}(1)+\frac{C_{2}}{(1)} \\
C_{1}+C_{2} & =6  \;\;\;...(i)\\
\frac{d y}{d x} & =C_{1}-\frac{C_{2}}{x^{2}}=2 \\
x & =1
\end{aligned}
[/latex] [latex]
C_{1}=C_{2}=2 [/latex] [latex]C_{1}=4, C_{2}=2 [/latex] [latex]y(x=2)=4(2)+\frac{2}{(2)}=9
[/latex]
explanation_html:
[latex] \frac{x d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}+\frac{x d y}{d x}-y=0, x \geq 1 [/latex]
This is an Euler-cauchy equation and has solutions of the form
[latex] \begin{aligned} & y=x^{n} \\ & y^{\prime}=n x^{n-1} \\ & y^{\prime \prime}=n(n-1) x^{n-2} \\ & x^{2}(n)(n-1) x^{n-2}+x\left(n x^{n-1}\right)-x^{n}=0 \\ & x^{n}[x(n-1)+n-1)=0 \\ & n^{2}-1=0 \\ & n=\pm 1 \\ & y_{1}=x \\ & y_{2}=\frac{1}{x} \\ & y=C_{1} x+\frac{C_{2}}{x} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Given [latex]y(x=1)=6[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} 6 & =C_{1}(1)+\frac{C_{2}}{(1)} \\ C_{1}+C_{2} & =6 \;\;\;...(i)\\ \frac{d y}{d x} & =C_{1}-\frac{C_{2}}{x^{2}}=2 \\ x & =1 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] C_{1}=C_{2}=2 [/latex]
[latex]C_{1}=4, C_{2}=2 [/latex]
[latex]y(x=2)=4(2)+\frac{2}{(2)}=9 [/latex]

subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
explanation_text: Given D.E. is [latex] \frac{du}{dx}=\frac{-xu^2}{2+x^2u}[/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow (2+x^2u)du+xu^2dx=0[/latex] Here [latex] M=xu^2 \;\;\;\;N=2+x^2u[/latex] [latex] \frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=2xu \;\;\;\;\;\frac{\partial M}{\partial x}=2xu [/latex] This is exact D.E General solution is [latex] \int_{\text{u constant}}Mdx+\int_{\text{term without 'x'}}Ndx=c[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \int (xu^2)dx+\int 2du=c [/latex] [latex] \therefore \; \frac{x^2u^2}{2}+2u=constant[/latex]
explanation_html:

[latex] \Rightarrow (2+x^2u)du+xu^2dx=0[/latex]
Here [latex] M=xu^2 \;\;\;\;N=2+x^2u[/latex]
[latex] \frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=2xu \;\;\;\;\;\frac{\partial M}{\partial x}=2xu [/latex]
This is exact D.E

explanation_text:

The system of linear equations in real [latex](x, y)[/latex] given
by [latex] (x\;\;y)\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 5-2\alpha \\ 
 \alpha & 1

non-trivial solutions for special value(s) of [latex]  \alpha  [/latex].
Which one or more among the following options is/

The system of linear equations in real [latex](x, y)[/latex] given by
[latex] (x\;\;y)\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5-2\alpha \\ \alpha & 1 \end{bmatrix} =(0\;\;0)[/latex]
involves a real parameter [latex] \alpha [/latex] and has infinitely many non-trivial solutions for special value(s) of [latex] \alpha [/latex]. explanation_html:
[latex] \begin{aligned} \begin{pmatrix} x &y \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 &5-2\alpha \\ \alpha & 1 \end{pmatrix}&=\begin{pmatrix} 0 &0 \end{pmatrix}\\ 2x+\alpha y&=0\\ (5-2\alpha )x+y&=0\\ \therefore \begin{pmatrix} 2 & \alpha \\ 5-2\alpha & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x\\y \end{pmatrix}&=\begin{pmatrix} 0\\0 \end{pmatrix} \;\;\; . . . . (1) \end{aligned}[/latex]
To get infinite number of non-trivial solutions [latex] \begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} 2 &\alpha \\ 5-2\alpha & 1 \end{vmatrix}&=0\\ 2-(5\alpha -2\alpha ^2)&=0\\ (2\alpha -1)(\alpha -2)&=0\\ \therefore \alpha =\frac{1}{2},\alpha &=2\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
At [latex]\alpha =\frac{1}{2} [/latex]; eq. (1) gives [latex](4x+y)=0 [/latex] . . .(2)
option (B) is satisfied by (2)
At [latex]\alpha =2 [/latex]; eq. (1) gives [latex](x+y)=0 [/latex] . . .(3)
option (A) is satisfied by (3)[latex] [/latex]
Both options (A) and (B) are correct

where [latex]i[/latex] is the imaginary unit, is
html:

evaluated over a counter-clockwise circular contour in the complex plane enclosing only the pole [latex]z = i[/latex], where [latex]i[/latex] is the imaginary unit, is
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
explanation_html: [latex] \begin{aligned} f(z)&=\frac{6z}{(2z^4-3\tau ^3+7\tau ^2-3x+5)}\\ &=\frac{6z}{(2z^4+2z^2)(5z^2+5)-3z^3-3z}\\ &=\frac{6z}{qz^2(z^2+1)+5(z^2+1)-3z(z^2+1)}\\ &=\frac{6z}{(z^2+1)(2z^2-3z+5)}\\ \therefore \oint f(z)dz&=2 \pi i \lim_{z \to 1}(z-i)f(z)\\ &=2\pi i \lim_{z \to i}\frac{6z}{(z+i)(2z^2-3z+5)}\\ &=2 \pi i \frac{6i}{2i(3-3i)}\\ &=\frac{2 \pi i}{(1-i)}\\ &=\pi(i-1) \end{aligned}[/latex]

html:

has a finite value for a real [latex]\alpha [/latex]. The value of [latex]\alpha [/latex] and the corresponding limit [latex]p [/latex] are
subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
explanation_text:
[latex] \begin{aligned}
 p&=\lim_{x \to \pi}\left ( \frac{x^2+\alpha x+2 \pi ^2}{x-\pi+2 \sin x} \right ) \\
p&=\left ( \frac{\pi ^2+\alpha \pi +2 \pi ^2}{\pi-\pi+2 \sin \pi } \right ) \\

 \therefore \;\; \alpha &= -3 \pi\\ 
 p&=\lim_{x \to \pi}\left ( \frac{x^2- 3 \pi x+2 \pi ^2}{x-\pi+2 \sin x} \right ) \\ 
 &=\lim_{x \to \pi}\left ( \frac{2x- 3 \pi }{1+2 \cos \pi} \right ) \\

explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Let}\qquad Q=\left[\begin{array}{ll}a & c \\c & b\end{array}\right], x&=\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\x_{2}\end{array}\right], R=\left[\begin{array}{l}r_{1} \\r_{2}\end{array}\right] \\ F(x)&=\frac{1}{2}\left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right)\left[\begin{array}{ll}a & c \\c & b\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\x_{2}\end{array}\right]-\left[r_{1} r_{2}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x_{1} \\x_{2}\end{array}\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[a x_{1}^{2}+b x_{2}^{2}+2 c x_{1} x_{2}\right]-\left[r_{1} x_{1}+r_{2} x_{2}\right]\\ \text{i.e.}\qquad \qquad U\left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right)&=\frac{1}{2} a x_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} b x_{2}^{2}+c_{1} x_{1} x_{2}-r_{1} x_{1}-r_{2} x_{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] Now, for critical point, [latex]\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_{1}}=0[/latex] and [latex]\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_{2}}=0[/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow \quad a_{1} x_{1}+c x_{2}-r_{1}=0 \quad \text { and } c x_{2}+c x_{1}-r_{2}=0[/latex] In matrix form we can write it as [latex] \begin{aligned} \left[\begin{array}{ll}a & c \\c & b\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} x_{1} \\m_{2}\end{array}\right] &=\left[\begin{array}{l}r_{1} \\ r_{2}\end{array}\right] \\\Rightarrow \qquad Q x &=r \end{aligned}[/latex] By multiplying both side by [latex]Q^{-1}[/latex] [latex] x=Q^{-1} r[/latex]
